quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on why sizing cost depends on count and on the language of trend lines and forecasts.

questions.q: Why does a finer warp (higher Ne) have more yarn surface to coat per kilogram?
options: Because finer yarn is more twisted
Because a kilogram of finer yarn contains more length
Because finer yarn absorbs less size
Because finer yarn has a larger diameter
questions.explain: Ne is length per unit weight, so a kilogram of Ne 40 holds twice the yards of Ne 20. More length means more surface, more size and more drying.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT given in the lecture as a reason sizing cost per kg rises with count?
options: More surface per kilogram must be coated
Finer yarn uses cheaper size chemicals
questions.explain: The lecture names surface area, higher add-on and slower machine speed. Cheaper chemicals is not a reason — and would lower, not raise, the cost.

questions.q: What does a trend line fitted by least squares do?
options: Finds the line or curve that minimises the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points
Draws the line through the first and last points
questions.explain: Least squares chooses the coefficients that make the squared residuals as small as possible. It does not pass through every point — the points scatter around it.

questions.q: The lecture's original table contained the sizing cost of 41 articles plotted against their warp count.
questions.explain: The lecture tabulated 41 articles; the worksheet loads a representative selection of 15 of those points.

questions.q: In the worksheet the trend fits are described as 'least squares over the 15 points'. The 15 points are:
options: A representative selection of the lecture's articles
questions.explain: The sheet loads a representative selection of the 41 articles so the student can type over them; the full-table fits quoted in the text use all 41.

questions.q: In the quadratic trend y = ax² + bx + c for sizing cost, x stands for:
questions.explain: The relationship is cost against warp count, so x is Ne and y is the forecast Rs/kg.

questions.q: The term 'forecast' in this lecture means:
options: Next year's price of size chemicals
The cost estimated from the trend for a count not in the table
The average cost of the 41 articles
questions.explain: FORECAST reads the fitted trend at a new x (e.g. Ne 40) to estimate what sizing a kilogram of that warp would cost.

questions.q: The double-pick article at 11.64 Rs/kg was excluded from both fits as an outlier.
questions.explain: The lecture states that both fits include the double-pick article at 11.64 Rs/kg; it was not removed.

questions.q: Which fit did the lecture judge to follow the data better?
options: The linear fit, because it is simpler
The quadratic fit, because it follows the upward curve
questions.explain: The quadratic bends upward with the data; the straight line under-estimates at both ends of the count range and over-estimates in the middle.

questions.q: The 'intercept' of the linear trend (3.3244 in the worksheet) represents:
options: The cost at Ne 0 on the fitted line
The cost of the finest article
The cost of a double-pick article
questions.explain: The intercept is the value of the line where x = 0. It has no physical warp, but it fixes the line's position; the slope (0.1422) gives the rise per count.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: Slopes, intercepts, curvature and the direction in which each forecast moves when the count changes.

questions.q: With a linear trend of slope 0.1422 Rs/kg per count, raising the warp count by 10 Ne raises the forecast sizing cost by about:
questions.explain: Slope × change in x = 0.1422 × 10 = Rs 1.42 per kg. Rs 3.32 is the intercept, which does not change with count.

questions.q: The linear forecast at warp count Ne is computed as:
questions.explain: A straight line is y = m x + c: 0.1422 × Ne + 3.3244. Swapping slope and intercept gives nonsense values at any count.

questions.q: A positive a-coefficient (x² term) in the quadratic fit means that:
options: Cost rises at a steadily decreasing rate with count
Cost rises more and more steeply as count rises
The curve is a straight line
questions.explain: A positive x² coefficient curves the trend upward, so each extra count adds more cost than the last — matching the steep climb of sizing cost at fine counts.

questions.q: For counts beyond Ne 40 the linear fit will give a higher forecast than the quadratic fit.
questions.explain: The lecture notes that the straight line under-estimates the cost beyond Ne 40; the upward-curving quadratic climbs faster and gives the higher figure there.

questions.q: In the middle of the count range the linear fit, compared with the quadratic, tends to:
questions.explain: A straight line through an upward-curving set of points sits above the curve in the middle and below it at the ends, so it over-estimates the middle counts.

questions.q: The quadratic forecast at count x uses which expression?
questions.explain: The lecture's form is 0.0027x² + 0.0172x + 4.4432, so a multiplies x², b multiplies x and c is the constant.

questions.q: If the sizing machine were speeded up for fine counts so that their cost no longer climbed so steeply, the fitted quadratic a-coefficient would:
questions.explain: The x² coefficient measures the curvature. Flattening the rise at fine counts reduces the curvature, so a becomes smaller.

questions.q: The units of the slope of the linear trend are rupees per kilogram per count.
questions.explain: Slope = change in y ÷ change in x = (Rs/kg) ÷ Ne, so each extra count adds 0.1422 Rs/kg in the worksheet fit.

questions.q: Two linear fits are made: one over 15 points (slope 0.1422, intercept 3.3244) and one over all 41 points giving 9.15 at Ne 40. Compared with the 15-point forecast of 9.01, the 41-point fit is:
questions.explain: 9.15 is above 9.01 at the same count, so the full-table line sits higher (or is steeper) there. Different point sets give different least-squares lines.

questions.q: At which count would the lecture's linear and quadratic trends be expected to differ least?
options: Around the middle of the range, where they cross
questions.explain: The line crosses the curve twice within the data range; near those crossings the two forecasts nearly agree, while at the extremes (Ne 7 or beyond 40) they diverge.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Evaluate the lecture's trend lines and use them to cost the sizing of real warp quantities.

questions.q: Using the worksheet linear fit, slope 0.1422 and intercept 3.3244, forecast the sizing cost at Ne 40 to two decimals (Rs/kg).
Using the same linear fit (slope 0.1422, intercept 3.3244), forecast the cost at Ne 30 to two decimals.
The lecture's full-table quadratic is 0.0027x² + 0.0172x + 4.4432. Evaluate it at Ne 40 to two decimals.
Evaluate the full-table quadratic 0.0027x² + 0.0172x + 4.4432 at Ne 20, to two decimals.
Evaluate the worksheet quadratic 0.00112x² + 0.0877x + 3.8597 at Ne 50, to two decimals.
At Ne 50, by how much does the worksheet quadratic (0.00112x² + 0.0877x + 3.8597) exceed the worksheet line (0.1422x + 3.3244)? Answer in Rs/kg to two decimals.
questions.explain: Quadratic 11.0447 − linear 10.4344 = 0.61 Rs/kg — the line already under-estimates beyond the data range.

questions.q: A warp of 1,200 kg of Ne 40 is to be sized. Using the full-table quadratic forecast of Rs 9.45 per kg, what is the sizing cost, to the nearest rupee?
With a linear slope of 0.1422 Rs/kg per count, by how many counts must the warp become finer for the forecast sizing cost to rise by exactly Rs 1 per kg? Answer to one decimal.
questions.explain: 1 ÷ 0.1422 = 7.03, so roughly every 7 counts adds a rupee per kilogram on the straight-line trend.

questions.q: An Ne 10 warp is forecast with the worksheet line (0.1422x + 3.3244). The result is about:
questions.explain: 0.1422 × 10 + 3.3244 = 4.7464 ≈ Rs 4.75. Rs 3.32 is only the intercept; Rs 4.89 is what the full-table quadratic gives at Ne 10.

questions.q: The line forecasts 9.15 and the quadratic 9.45 at Ne 40 for a 2,000 kg warp. The difference in budgeted sizing cost is:
questions.explain: (9.45 − 9.15) × 2,000 = 0.30 × 2,000 = Rs 600 — the amount the straight line would under-budget.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Using the sizing-cost trend in the costing office: quoting new counts, checking budgets and spotting bad fits.

questions.q: A buyer asks for a quotation on an Ne 40 warp the mill has never sized. The best use of the lecture's analysis is to:
options: Use the cost of the nearest Ne 20 article
Read the quadratic trend at Ne 40 as the sizing cost per kg
Use the average of all 41 articles
Assume sizing cost is independent of count
questions.explain: The trend was fitted exactly for this purpose; the quadratic follows the steep rise at fine counts. An Ne 20 cost or an average would badly under-quote.

questions.q: A costing clerk uses the linear trend to quote an Ne 60 warp. The likely consequence is:
options: An over-quote, because the line is too steep
An under-quote, because the line falls below the real curve beyond Ne 40
No error — the line is exact above Ne 40
questions.explain: The lecture notes the straight line under-estimates beyond Ne 40, and Ne 60 is far outside the data, so the real cost will be higher than the line predicts.

questions.q: A new article is a double-pick quality whose actual sizing cost came out at 11.64 Rs/kg, above the trend. Before quoting the next similar article you should:
options: Delete the point as a mistake
Note that this construction sizes dearer than the count alone predicts, and allow for it
Lower the forecast to the trend value
questions.explain: The trend captures count only; construction features such as double picks add cost. The lecture kept the point in the fit, and a planner should keep the lesson too.

questions.q: If a mill's sizing data shows no upward curvature, a linear trend would be a perfectly reasonable forecasting tool for counts inside the data range.
questions.explain: The quadratic is preferred only because the lecture's data curves upward. Where the points lie close to a straight line, the simpler model forecasts well within its range.

questions.q: To cut the sizing cost per kg of a fine Ne 60 warp, which action attacks a cause named in the lecture?
options: Increase the width of the fabric
Increase the sizing machine speed without losing size quality
questions.explain: Slower machine speed on fine counts is one of the three named causes; a faster run spreads machine cost over more kilograms. Weft and looms do not affect warp sizing cost.

questions.q: A planner budgets sizing at a flat Rs 6 per kg for every article. Which articles will be most under-budgeted?
options: None — the flat rate is safe
questions.explain: At Ne 40 the trend gives over Rs 9 per kg, so a flat Rs 6 under-budgets by more than Rs 3 per kg; coarse counts near Rs 4–5 would actually be over-budgeted.

questions.q: An article's sizing cost is quoted per kilogram of warp. For a fabric costing per metre, this must be multiplied by:
options: The warp weight per metre in kg
questions.explain: Cost per kg × kg of warp per metre gives sizing cost per metre of fabric — the figure used later in feasibility costing. Weft is not sized.

questions.q: Replacing the 15 worksheet points with your own mill's data will change the slope and intercept of the fit automatically.
questions.explain: The fit cells are formulas over the input points; new data gives a new least-squares line and curve, which is how the sheet is meant to be used.

questions.q: A mill's own data gives a quadratic with a NEGATIVE a-coefficient. What does this suggest?
options: Sizing cost accelerates at fine counts
The rise in cost flattens out at fine counts, which contradicts the usual pattern and should be checked
questions.explain: A negative x² term bends the curve downward, meaning fine counts get cheaper to size at the margin — the reverse of the lecture's experience, so the data or the fit deserve a second look.

questions.q: Which quantity, added to the count, would most improve the forecasting of sizing cost for an unusual article?
options: The total ends and picks per inch (construction density) and whether it is double-pick
questions.explain: The off-trend article in the lecture was a double-pick construction; density features explain variation that count alone cannot. Customer and colour have no bearing on sizing.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder reasoning about fits, residuals and extrapolation, with the arithmetic errors students most often make.

questions.q: For the worksheet quadratic 0.00112x² + 0.0877x + 3.8597, the printed forecast at Ne 40 is 9.17. Evaluate the formula at Ne 40 with these rounded coefficients, to two decimals.
questions.explain: 1.792 + 3.508 + 3.8597 = 9.1597 → 9.16. The sheet shows 9.17 because it uses unrounded coefficients; rounding the coefficients shifts the last decimal.

questions.q: A student evaluates 0.0027x² at Ne 40 as 0.0027 × 40 × 2 = 0.216. The correct value and the error are:
questions.explain: x² = 1,600, so 0.0027 × 1,600 = 4.32. Treating the square as a doubling is a very common slip that wrecks the forecast.

questions.q: Using the full-table quadratic 0.0027x² + 0.0172x + 4.4432, how much more does it cost to size 1 kg of Ne 40 than 1 kg of Ne 20? Answer to two decimals.
questions.explain: Ne 40: 9.4512; Ne 20: 5.8672; difference 3.584 → Rs 3.58 per kg — the finer count costs about 61 % more to size.

questions.q: On the lecture's full table the line gives 9.15 and the quadratic 9.45 at Ne 40, yet at Ne 7 the line also lies below the curve. How can a line lie below a curve at both ends?
options: It cannot — one figure must be wrong
The curve is convex (bends upward), so a straight line fitted through it crosses it twice and lies below at both ends
Because the data have only 15 points
questions.explain: An upward-curving set of points sits below its best-fit line in the middle and above it at the extremes. That is exactly why the lecture says the line under-estimates at both ends.

questions.q: A quadratic fit always gives a better forecast than a linear fit, whatever the data.
questions.explain: A quadratic always fits the given points at least as closely, but with few points or noisy data it can bend to follow noise and extrapolate badly; the lecture prefers it here because the data genuinely curve upward.

questions.q: A fine warp of Ne 40 weighs 0.30 lb per metre of fabric. Using Rs 9.45 per kg, what is the sizing cost per metre of fabric to two decimals? (1 kg = 2.2046 lb)
questions.explain: 0.30 lb ÷ 2.2046 = 0.1361 kg of warp per metre; × 9.45 = Rs 1.29 per metre.

questions.q: The worksheet's 15-point line forecasts 9.01 at Ne 40 and the 41-point line 9.15. A planner wants a single figure to quote. The soundest choice is:
options: 9.01, the lower and therefore safer price
9.45 from the full-table quadratic, since it follows the curve and uses all the data
questions.explain: The full table with the quadratic uses the most data and the better-fitting shape. Quoting the lowest line forecast would under-recover the real sizing cost.

questions.q: Using the worksheet line (slope 0.1422, intercept 3.3244), at what count does the forecast reach Rs 12 per kg? Answer to the nearest whole count.
questions.explain: (12 − 3.3244) ÷ 0.1422 = 61.0, so around Ne 61 on the straight line — far beyond the data, where the real curve would reach Rs 12 sooner.

questions.q: An article of Ne 20 shows an actual cost of 7.50 Rs/kg against a trend value of 5.87. The residual of +1.63 most probably reflects:
options: A fault in the least-squares method
A construction effect such as a dense or double-pick warp that needs higher add-on
That Ne 20 is outside the data range
That the intercept is too high
questions.explain: Residuals are what count alone cannot explain; the lecture's own off-trend point was a double-pick article. Ne 20 is well inside the range and the method is sound.

questions.q: Which statement about the two worksheet fits is correct at Ne 7, the coarsest count?
options: The line (4.32) is above the quadratic (4.53)
The quadratic (4.53) is above the line (4.32)
questions.explain: Line: 0.1422 × 7 + 3.3244 = 4.32; quadratic: 0.00112 × 49 + 0.0877 × 7 + 3.8597 = 4.53. At the coarse end the line sits below the curve, as the lecture says.
